title: What I Actually Use
metaTitle: What I Actually Use — Tools I Reorder
metaDescription: The short list: the tools, supplements and gear that have survived months in my real routine, with a one-line reason for each.
intro: This is the short list. Everything on this page has survived at least three months in my actual routine, not a sample box and not a one week trial. If something stops earning its place, it comes off the page, which is why this collection stays deliberately small. I have grouped it the way I would hand it to a friend who asked what I would buy again: the supplement I reorder without thinking, the software that makes a work day quieter, and the two or three pieces of gear I would replace the same afternoon if they broke. Prices move around constantly. The list itself moves very slowly, and that is the entire point of keeping it.

faq.q: How does something get on this list?
faq.a: I have to have paid for it myself and used it for at least three months. Gifted product can be reviewed, but it does not get listed here until I have lived with it long enough to reorder it.

faq.q: Do you take money to add products?
faq.a: No. Placement is never for sale. I do earn a commission when you buy through a link on this page, which never changes your price.

faq.q: Why is the list so short?
faq.a: Because a list of forty favourites is not a list of favourites. Anything that stops getting used gets removed, so what is left is genuinely what I reach for.

title: The Creator Stack
metaTitle: The Creator Stack — Tools I Publish With
metaDescription: The software I use to write, film, edit, caption and send: the full creator stack, with an honest note on what each tool is actually for.
intro: Every tool on this page is part of how a post actually gets made, from the first script to the email that goes out after it. I am picky here for a boring reason: software is a subscription, so a bad choice costs you every month until you notice. What follows is the stack I run week to week, with the specific job each tool does and where it stops being worth the money. Where a cheaper option does the same work I have said so, and where I have cancelled something after a few months I have left the note in. Start with one tool, not the whole page.

faq.q: Do I need all of these?
faq.a: No, and buying the whole stack at once is the fastest way to waste money. Pick the one tool that removes your current bottleneck, run it for a month, then decide.
For most of these, yes, and for editing and design the free tiers are genuinely usable for a long time. I have noted where paying actually bought me back hours.

faq.q: Do these links cost me more?
faq.a: No. Signing up through a link here is the same price as going direct, and in a few cases the partner link carries a trial or discount that the public page does not.

title: Calm Tools
metaTitle: Calm Tools — Sleep, Breath and Recovery
metaDescription: Sleep, breathwork, recovery and the two supplements I actually reorder. No miracle claims, just what measurably changed my evenings.
intro: This collection is about the end of the day rather than the start of it. Sleep, breathwork, recovery and the two supplements I still reorder after a couple of years. I want to be careful here, because this is the corner of the internet where the claims get loudest and the evidence gets thinnest, so nothing on this page is described as a cure for anything. What each item gets is a plain sentence about what changed for me and how long it took. Most of it is unglamorous: darkness, temperature, a consistent wind down, magnesium. If you buy one thing, make it the cheapest one first.

faq.q: Is any of this medical advice?
faq.a: No. I am a creator, not a clinician. Talk to a doctor before starting any supplement, especially if you take medication or you are pregnant.
The eye mask. It is the cheapest item here and it did more for my sleep than anything else on the page, which is slightly annoying to admit.
Give a sleep change two full weeks before you judge it. Almost everything here felt like nothing for the first few nights.

title: Morning Routine
metaTitle: Morning Routine — Coffee, Light and Pages
metaDescription: The small, repeatable morning kit: coffee gear, light, water and the notebook. Things that make the first hour easier to repeat.
intro: A morning routine is mostly a set of objects that make the first hour easy to repeat. That is the whole theory behind this page. Coffee gear that works before you are properly awake, light that arrives on a timer instead of a decision, water that you will actually drink, and a notebook small enough that writing three lines does not feel like a project. None of this is a system and none of it will fix a bad night, which is why the calm tools page comes first in my own order of operations. What is here is durable, mostly inexpensive, and forgiving of the mornings when you skip it entirely.

faq.q: What is the single highest leverage item here?
faq.a: The kettle, if you make coffee daily. Temperature control turned a variable cup into a repeatable one, which removed a small decision from every morning.

faq.q: Do I need the expensive coffee setup?
faq.a: No. The press on this page costs under forty dollars and gets ninety percent of the way there. Buy the grinder before you upgrade the brewer.

title: Desk Setup
metaTitle: Desk Setup — Camera, Light, Sound, Chair
metaDescription: The desk that films, records and holds up to eight-hour days: chair, light, mic, monitor arm and the cables that stopped the chaos.
intro: This desk has to do two jobs: hold up to long working days and be filmable at short notice. Those goals fight each other more than you would expect, so most of the choices here are compromises I have made on purpose and can defend. The chair is the one place I would tell anyone to overspend, because it is the only item you are in contact with for eight hours. Lighting matters more than the camera, sound matters more than the lighting, and cable management matters more than all of it for whether the setup still looks good in six months. Buy in that order.

faq.a: Lighting, every time. A phone camera in good light beats a mirrorless camera in bad light, and the light costs a fraction as much.

faq.q: Is a standing desk worth it?
faq.a: Only if you will actually change position. If it stays at one height all year, a solid fixed desk and a better chair is the smarter spend.
Sound is the first thing people notice and the last thing anyone budgets for. A dynamic mic in an untreated room beats a condenser almost every time.

title: Under $25
metaTitle: Under $25 — Small Things That Earn It
metaDescription: Everything here is under twenty-five dollars and still in weekly use: the small, unglamorous things that quietly earn their place.
intro: Small things, none of them over twenty five dollars, all still in weekly use. I like this page because the low price makes it honest: nothing here can hide behind being an investment, so it either gets used or it gets cut. A lot of what ends up in this collection is consumable or nearly disposable, which is exactly why the specific version matters more than it does with expensive gear. The wrong five dollar cable is genuinely worse than the right one, and you will notice every day. If you have never bought anything I recommend, start here rather than with the expensive pages.

faq.q: Why does the exact version matter at this price?
faq.a: Because cheap categories are where the quality range is widest. The difference between a good and bad five dollar cable is total, and the price tells you nothing.

faq.q: Do prices stay under twenty five dollars?
faq.a: Not always. Prices drift, and when something settles above the line for good it moves to another collection rather than sitting here misleading you.
